# True or false: Reliability

SLOs, on-call, incidents, rollbacks and backups. Several of these statements sound responsible and make outages longer.

11 statements (Foundation 7, Standard 4). Decide whether each one is true or false before you open the answer. Every answer says why and links to the page that teaches it.

Prefer the terminal? From the repository root, run `python3 exercises/quiz.py --area reliability`.

### 1. A 100% availability SLO shows users that you take reliability seriously.

Level: Foundation

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** A 100% target leaves no error budget for any change, so it either stops all releases or gets ignored. No dependency you rely on achieves 100% either. Set the target from your last 4 weeks of data and what users tolerate.

Read more: [playbook/reliability/service-levels.md](../../playbook/reliability/service-levels.md)

</details>

### 2. A 99.9% SLO over 28 days allows about 40 minutes of full outage.

Level: Foundation

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** The error budget is 0.1% of 28 days, which is about 40 minutes. At 99.99% it drops to about 4 minutes. Every extra nine costs much more to reach, so choose the target users need.

Read more: [playbook/reliability/service-levels.md](../../playbook/reliability/service-levels.md)

</details>

### 3. Paging on-call engineers when CPU passes 90% is good practice.

Level: Foundation

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** Users feel failed or slow requests, not CPU. Page on symptoms, ideally on SLO burn rate, and send resource alerts to dashboards or tickets. On-call people who get paged for noise soon start ignoring pages.

Read more: [playbook/reliability/service-levels.md](../../playbook/reliability/service-levels.md)

</details>

### 4. Every incident has one root cause, and the goal of analysis is to find it.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** In complex systems, failures need several things to go wrong at once: a change, a missing test, a quiet alert, a deadline. Fixing only the last step leaves the others in place for the next incident. Look for the set of contributing factors.

Read more: [playbook/reliability/root-cause-analysis.md](../../playbook/reliability/root-cause-analysis.md)

</details>

### 5. The 5 Whys, used on its own, is enough to analyse a serious incident.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** Used alone, the 5 Whys follows a single chain and usually stops at a person or one bug. Treat it as a starting prompt. For serious incidents, build a timeline and list contributing factors, and add a fishbone diagram or CAST when the cause is disputed.

Read more: [playbook/reliability/root-cause-analysis.md](../../playbook/reliability/root-cause-analysis.md)

</details>

### 6. 'Human error' is an acceptable root cause in a postmortem.

Level: Foundation

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** People make mistakes in every system, so 'human error' explains nothing you can fix. Ask what made the error possible, easy and uncaught. Those conditions are the contributing factors to fix.

Read more: [playbook/reliability/postmortems.md](../../playbook/reliability/postmortems.md)

</details>

### 7. When a recent change causes an incident, the default should be to roll back rather than fix forward.

Level: Foundation

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** Undoing the last change is the fastest way to end most incidents. Roll forward only when the fix is known, small, already reviewed and in production within 30 minutes. If someone is still 'nearly there' after 30 minutes, roll back.

Read more: [playbook/reliability/rollbacks.md](../../playbook/reliability/rollbacks.md)

</details>

### 8. A weekly change advisory board makes production changes safer than peer review plus automated testing.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** The research behind the DORA metrics found that approval by an external body did not improve stability and was linked to slower delivery. Peer review plus automated testing did better. Keep a board only for the few changes that carry risk across teams.

Read more: [playbook/reliability/change-management.md](../../playbook/reliability/change-management.md)

</details>

### 9. Database replication to a second site counts as a backup.

Level: Foundation

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** Replication copies deletions and ransomware encryption to the second site within seconds. Keep separate, versioned backups, with one copy that attackers cannot change or delete. Replication helps availability; backups help recovery.

Read more: [playbook/reliability/backup-and-recovery.md](../../playbook/reliability/backup-and-recovery.md)

</details>

### 10. A backup that has never been restored should not be counted as a backup.

Level: Foundation

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** Until you restore it, you do not know whether the backup is complete or how long recovery takes. The playbook calls an untested backup a hope, not a control. Restore Tier 1 data automatically every month and time it against the RTO.

Read more: [playbook/reliability/backup-and-recovery.md](../../playbook/reliability/backup-and-recovery.md)

</details>

### 11. A sustainable on-call rotation means nobody carries the pager more than one week in six.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** That needs at least six people in the rotation. Three people covering every night burn out and then leave. Merge rotations, move to business hours or hire, rather than asking for heroics.

Read more: [playbook/reliability/on-call.md](../../playbook/reliability/on-call.md)

</details>
